intro: Michael Laucke places Satie’s piano texture on six guitar strings, in a different key. Follow how each plucked bass, chord and melodic note carries into the space before the next attack; the recording is licensed CC BY-SA 4.0, not a public-domain sound recording.
question: How does a plucked string carry Satie’s held melody across the changing accompaniment?

cues.title: Six strings, another key
cues.text: This is Laucke’s guitar arrangement, not Satie’s piano original. The music sounds in A rather than the piano version’s D: compare the spacing of bass and upper notes, not their absolute register.
cues.evidence: Commons identifies Laucke’s arrangement and performance. The delivered comparison map records transposeB -5: the guitar’s pitch-class features are rotated five semitones upwards to correspond with the piano reference. This establishes a pitch-class correspondence, not the exact octave of every voice; playback remains unchanged.

cues.title: A melody between plucks
cues.text: Follow the melodic line across the repeated plucks below it. Laucke’s opening has a pronounced rise and retreat around the melody’s early phrases; a held note has to remain audible while fresh attacks renew the accompaniment.
cues.evidence: The report rises from −17.2 dB at 0:05 to −10.7 at 0:10, then falls to −17.4 at 0:15. The piano score distinguishes held melody from recurring accompaniment; the guitar source documents its adaptation. No particular finger, string or melodic entry is identified.

cues.title: The bass changes the colour
cues.text: In this stretch, follow the lower notes as the opening alternation gives way to the next phrase. The guitar keeps bass, chord and melody within one player’s reach; notice which part remains clear as the harmony changes.
cues.evidence: The report has a boundary at 0:36. The piano reference’s bar-19 modal turn at 42.928 seconds maps provisionally to about 37.5 here after correcting the five-semitone transposition. Mutopia 37 supplies the underlying piano form, not a guitar fingering or exact voicing.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Room before the return
cues.text: The first traversal eases towards its ending before the opening begins again. Listen to how Laucke separates the last sustained sounds from the next bass-and-chord pattern, rather than treating every quiet interval as a new phrase.
cues.evidence: The 1:04 and 1:20 boundaries frame this closing region. The level falls from −13.8 dB at 1:10 to −20.3 at 1:20; the provisional piano-to-guitar map places the repeat near 1:22.3. The cue covers the approach, not an exact release.

cues.title: The opening, plucked again
cues.text: The opening material returns. Compare the familiar accompaniment with its first appearance: the melody must still connect across notes that are attacked separately and then allowed to diminish.
cues.evidence: The piano score repeats its opening after the first ending; reference time 90.34 maps to approximately 82.3 seconds here. A strong guitar boundary at 1:20 and the quieter 1:20–1:25 region support this approximate placement. The map is automatic, not checked by ear.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A different route home
cues.text: The second ending changes the harmony rather than merely repeating the first close. Keep the bass in mind while the upper notes take another route; the changed ending survives the move from piano to guitar.
cues.evidence: Mutopia 37 has different first and second endings. Its second-ending start at reference 158.528 seconds maps to 148.8 here, beside the guitar report’s 2:30 boundary. This supports the region; the arrangement’s exact voicings have not been score-aligned.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: After the last pluck
cues.text: The closing sound diminishes without another phrase beginning. Listen past the attack into its decay: on this recording, the disappearance of the tone occupies a different space from the earlier pauses between plucks.
cues.evidence: The report falls from −15.6 dB at 2:40 to −26.0 at 2:45 and −60.4 at 2:50, with no detected onsets in the last window. These measurements locate the closing decay, not an exact finger release.

transitions.title: The bass leaves its opening alternation
transitions.how: Satie’s repeated two-chord accompaniment gives way to a moving bass route and a lower held melody note. Laucke carries that change into the guitar arrangement without replacing the bass-and-chord pulse. Follow the harmony beneath the long note rather than expecting a new tune at every pluck.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia 37, piano bars 17–21, supplies the underlying change. Reference bar 19 at 42.928 seconds maps to 37.5 here; the guitar has a boundary at 0:36. No guitar fingering or exact octave is asserted.

transitions.title: An ending clears the opening pattern
transitions.how: The first ending settles before the original accompaniment returns. The melody waits while the bass and chord pattern re-establish the opening. On guitar, listen for the distinction between the resonance left by the ending and the fresh attacks that restart the pattern.
transitions.evidence: The piano score’s opening return at 90.34 seconds maps provisionally to 82.3 here. The guitar’s 1:20 boundary and low level around 1:20 support the region. Timing is not a manually checked bar alignment.

transitions.title: A familiar phrase changes its ending
transitions.how: The repeated body reaches a different closing phrase. In the piano original, the second ending substitutes a minor third for the major third heard at the first close. Compare the destination of Laucke’s upper line with the earlier ending, while the accompaniment retains its measured pattern.
transitions.evidence: Mutopia 37, alternatives at bars 32–39 and 40–47, documents the piano endings. The second-ending boundary maps from 158.528 to approximately 148.8 seconds; the guitar report has a 2:30 novelty boundary. The description distinguishes score evidence from the provisional guitar timing.

composer.background:
Satie was born in the Norman port of Honfleur to a French father and a Scottish mother. After his mother died in 1872, he lived with his paternal grandparents and received lessons from a local organist. He later joined his father in Paris and entered the Conservatoire in 1879. His periods of study ended without the normal professional qualifications. His mature music would expose elementary actions — a bass note, a repeated chord, a scale fragment.

By the late 1880s he was working in Montmartre, including at the Chat Noir cabaret. The three Sarabandes of 1887 and Gymnopédies of 1888 came from this period. The latter use a slow triple metre, low bass notes and chords on the second beat. Major sevenths remain part of the sonority instead of being immediately corrected into consonances. Their regular accompaniment continues beneath a melody whose phrase-endings often avoid the sort of cadence that would make the next phrase feel inevitable.
composer.epithet: A cabaret pianist who separated repetition from development, and musical seriousness from ceremonial behaviour.
